issues.legal_issue: A party that agreed to an appellate court deciding the merits on the existing record cannot later deny the recorded agreement without first seeking correction of the record.
material_facts: The parties agreed before the High Court that it would decide the merits on the existing record rather than remand the case.
The High Court recorded that agreement and decided the merits.
The appellant later denied having agreed, but had not asked the High Court to correct its record.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not contradict the High Court’s record of the agreement, and the challenge to the High Court’s course of proceeding failed.
issues.legal_principle: Under State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak and Bhavnagar University v. Palitana Sugar Mill Pvt. Ltd., statements in a judgment recording what transpired in court are conclusive unless the party promptly asks the judges who made the record to correct it.

predicates.appeal_challenges_recorded_consent: A party in an appeal disputes the appellate court’s account that the parties agreed to a course of proceeding.
predicates.parties_agreed_to_merits_decision_withou: The parties agreed that the appellate court would decide the merits on the existing record rather than send the case back for reconsideration.
predicates.no_prompt_record_correction_request: The party disputing the account did not promptly ask the judges who made the record to correct it.

issues.definition: When an appeal disputes a recorded agreement, the party cannot deny that agreement if the parties agreed to the merits decision without remand and no prompt request was made to correct the record.

issues.legal_issue: Oral evidence may be given to show that a written document was not intended to operate as an agreement but was a sham.
material_facts: The appellant asserted that the written agency-and-licence agreement was a sham and was not intended to be acted upon.
Evidence showed that the appellant submitted accounts and paid commissions in accordance with the agreement.
The appellant’s account of why the agreement was allegedly a sham was rejected on the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The bar on varying written terms did not prevent oral evidence to show that the document was a sham, although the evidence in this case did not establish that claim.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, require the writing to prove its terms and generally bar oral evidence that contradicts or varies those terms. They do not bar a party from proving that a document was never intended to operate as an agreement and was merely a sham. The Court relied on Smt. Gangabai v. Smt. Chhabubai and Ishwar Dass Jain v. Sohan Lal.

predicates.dispute_over_written_agreement: The proceeding concerns the effect of a written agreement between parties.
predicates.party_claims_document_was_sham: A party asserts that the written document was not intended to operate as an agreement and was only a sham.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a written agreement, a party claiming that the document was a sham may lead oral evidence to prove that claim.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement providing for commission-based business and accounting, without a fixed monthly payment, may establish a licence rather than a lease when the evidence shows that it was acted upon.
material_facts: The written agreement provided for commission on tailoring and sales and required separate accounts.
The appellant rendered accounts and made payments corresponding to the stated commissions.
The agreement specified no fixed monthly rent, and the evidence supported the conclusion that the appellant used the premises under a licence rather than a lease.
issues.conclusion: The agreement created a licence, not a lease, and the appellant was a licensee rather than a lessee.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the distinction between a lease and a licence by considering the agreement and the parties’ conduct. Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act governed proof of the written terms and the limits on varying them; Delta International Ltd. v. Shyam Sundar Ganeriwalla was also considered in relation to tenancy rights and the ability to create a sub-tenancy.

predicates.civil_possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns the right to possess premises under an arrangement between the parties.
predicates.written_arrangement_sets_commissions_and: The written arrangement provides for commission-based business and requires accounts to be kept or rendered.
predicates.parties_performed_commission_and_account: The occupant rendered accounts or made payments consistent with the commission arrangement.
predicates.no_fixed_periodic_rent: The arrangement does not require a fixed periodic rent for the premises.

issues.definition: In a civil possession dispute, an occupancy arrangement is a licence rather than a lease when its written terms provide for commission and accounting, those terms were performed, and no fixed periodic rent was set.

issues.legal_issue: A sub-tenancy that requires the original landlord’s consent cannot be asserted when that consent was not given.
material_facts: The appellant claimed to occupy the premises as a sub-tenant.
The original landlord had not consented to the creation of a sub-tenancy.
The asserted sub-tenancy was therefore prohibited by the applicable rent-control law.
issues.conclusion: The plea of sub-tenancy was rightly rejected because the original landlord had not consented to it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, prohibited the relevant sub-tenancy without the original landlord’s consent. The Court relied on Waman Shriniwas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas and Co. for the principle that a subletting made without required consent is unlawful and cannot be enforced, and considered Delta International Ltd. v. Shyam Sundar Ganeriwalla concerning a tenant’s inability to confer a better tenancy interest than the tenant possesses.

predicates.subtenancy_claim_in_possession_dispute: A person claims a right to occupy premises as a sub-tenant in a possession dispute.
predicates.applicable_rule_requires_original_landlo: The governing rule makes the creation of the claimed sub-tenancy dependent on the original landlord’s consent.
predicates.original_landlord_did_not_consent: The original landlord did not consent to the claimed sub-tenancy.

issues.definition: A sub-tenancy claim in a possession dispute is rejected as unlawful when the governing rule requires the original landlord’s consent and that consent was not given.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may enhance damages for use and occupation when it has authority to determine the matter with the parties’ consent and the record supports the increased amount.
material_facts: The parties consented to the High Court deciding the merits and exercising its appellate powers under Order 41, Rules 30, 32 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
The High Court found that the premises would ordinarily have generated a higher monthly amount than the trial court had awarded.
The evidence and the parties’ position supported the High Court’s assessment of the amount for use and occupation.
The appellant challenged the enhancement, but the Supreme Court found no basis to interfere.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s enhanced award of damages for use and occupation was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, Rules 30, 32 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, empowered the High Court to decide the appeal and make an appropriate decree; in this case the parties consented to its exercise of those powers. The Court upheld the assessment because the record supported the increased damages.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerns_use_and_occupation: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil dispute that includes damages for use and occupation of premises.
predicates.parties_consent_to_appellate_merits_deci: The parties consent to the appellate court deciding the merits and exercising its appellate powers to make a decree.
predicates.record_supports_higher_compensation: The evidence supports a higher amount of compensation for use and occupation than the amount fixed below.

issues.definition: An appellate court may award higher use-and-occupation damages in a civil appeal when the parties consent to its merits decision and the record supports higher compensation.
